## The map

**Map review (decided 21 October 2026, built with the redrawn seas in build order item 7).** The map's density follows the politics: the Levant, where most of the Amarna letters were written, is finely divided, and Anatolia and Mesopotamia coarsely. That is right for the game, with these corrections:

- **Distance, not steps.** Each connection gets a length, weighted by its terrain, so travel time follows the ground rather than the number of provinces between. Two steps on the Anatolian plateau cover far more ground than two along the Levantine coast.
- **The northern Syrian theatre.** Northern Syria was the battleground of Hatti, Mitanni and Egypt in exactly this period. Add Aleppo (Halab), the great city of the north, in Mitanni's sphere until the Hittites took it, and Qatna, whose king Akizzi wrote several of the letters; and, since the redrawn seas need them, Sidon and the island of Arwad. Ṣumur, Egypt's base on Amurru's coast and the city of the Arwad blockade, is built both ways and the better one kept: as Amurru's harbour, or as a province of its own. The only argument against its own province is how crowded the coast becomes on a phone, and that is the interface's to solve, not the period's to give up: Ṣumur is a province of its own, the city Abdi-Ashirta and Aziru took and Rib-Hadda begged Pharaoh to save, and the phone is made to read it ("Map on small screens"; decided 27 October 2026, answering item 7a's review, where it had been kept as Amurru's harbour because four cities' names touched at the first zoom step on a 390-pixel screen). The long Carchemish–Qadesh link then gives way to links through them.
- **Places in their own time.** Mari was destroyed by Hammurabi around 1760 BCE and by 1346 was a small place in the land of Hana, so the middle Euphrates province takes a name of its period and loses Mari's fortress walls. Kanesh mattered mostly in the earlier Old Assyrian age, so its province takes a name of the Hittite period. Ekallatum is likewise best known from the Old Assyrian age, and Tamassos from the Iron Age: Cyprus keeps two provinces, each named for a town of the period like every other province. The east keeps Enkomi, the great harbour town and probably the seat of the king of Alashiya. The west, with Morphou Bay, where ships from Anatolia and Crete came ashore, and the copper hills, takes the name of a Late Bronze Age town inside the area it covers: Toumba tou Skourou if it centres on Morphou Bay and the copper hills, Palaepaphos (Kouklia) if it reaches the southwest coast, Kalavasos if it takes in the south. No region is removed; only names out of their time change, and the builder draws each province first, then chooses its name from the sources and records the basis.
- **Connections of the right kind.** The routes from the middle Euphrates to Damascus and Qadesh cross the Syrian desert and become desert connections. Kanesh–Carchemish crosses mountains and gets a pass, as Kanesh–Kizzuwatna has.
- **Nubia.** Kush, south of Thebes, was the source of Egypt's gold, the gold every other Great King asked for ("gold is as plentiful as dirt in your land", Tushratta wrote), and was governed directly by Egypt's viceroy, the King's Son of Kush. It joins the map as Egyptian land: the Nile runs through it, its land is arid and carries few people, and its yield is mostly gold. From item 11+ scoring measures each power against par for its starting position ("One scoreboard for every power" under Victory), so a richer Egypt also faces a higher bar; the balance pass watches Egypt's start, as "Opening relations as they were" already asks.

Also:

- **What earns a place.** A province is a polity or administrative centre that acts in the period's diplomacy or war, not a town above some size. By that bar add Alalakh (Mukish), a Mitanni vassal and Idrimi's city; Nuhashshe, fought over in Suppiluliuma's Syrian wars; two provinces for southern Canaan's highlands, Jerusalem under Abdi-Heba and Shechem under Labaya, rival vassals of Egypt who accused each other before Pharaoh of joining the Habiru, which is the kind of story the game is built to produce (if the coast and highlands grow crowded on a phone, the interface is made to read them first: "Map on small screens"); and Arrapha, Mitanni's eastern vassal, whose town of Nuzi left the adoption tablets. With the edges below, the map then has about 54 to 56 land provinces, most of the new ones in Syria and Canaan, so item 7a's review checks the map on a phone, the Levant above all. Labaya was probably dead by 1346; he starts the game anyway, a stretch of about five years marked in the dossier, for the story (decided 27 October 2026, answering item 6+'s review). Kumidi in the Beqaa, the third of Egypt's administrative centres in Canaan beside Gaza and Ṣumur, stays within Damascus's land: an Egyptian commissioner's seat under Biryawaza (EA 194-197), it did not act as a polity of its own (decided 27 October 2026, answering item 7a's review). By the same bar, six cities of Canaan that act in the letters but sat inside larger provinces join the map as city-states, now that the phone reads the Levant by zooming (decided 29 October 2026, build order item 11c; "The map in true geography, and its look in time" under Interface): Akko, whose men killed Babylon's merchants (EA 8) and whose ruler Surata let Labaya go for a bribe (EA 245); Hazor, the largest town in Canaan, whose ruler Abdi-Tirshi called himself king (EA 227-228); Gezer under Milkilu and Shuwardata's land in the southern hills, both accused before Pharaoh by Abdi-Heba of giving the king's land to the Habiru (EA 287, 289); Lachish under Zimreddi; and Ashkelon under Yidya. The same bar leaves Crete off the map (decided 21 October 2026, "The Aegean's far shore" under Ideas). Read again against the map in true geography, the same bar adds six more places (decided 29 October 2026, build order item 11f): Azzi-Hayasa, the highlands beyond Isuwa, whose lord Hukkana swore a treaty with Suppiluliuma and married his sister, and where Hatti fought its north-eastern war; Tunip on the Orontes, whose citizens wrote to Pharaoh as one, begging for help against Aziru (EA 59); Niya on the Orontes under Takuwa, caught up in Suppiluliuma's first Syrian war; Beirut under Ammunira (EA 141-143), where Rib-Hadda fled when his brother shut him out of Byblos, carved from the land of Byblos and Sidon that holds it today; and Pella under Mut-Bahlu and Ashtaroth under Ayyab, east of the Jordan, tangled up with Labaya's sons (EA 255-256); with Samuha, in Hatti's Upper Land, where the Hittite court sat while Hattusa was overrun, as Hatti's own province. Wilusa, Hapalla and Masa, which act mostly a generation later, stay drawn and named as lands outside the game.
- **Historical routes and times.** Connections follow known routes: the coast road to Egypt, the King's Highway east of the Jordan, the Euphrates route and the Taurus passes. Travel times are calibrated against journeys the sources attest where they give them, and the builder records what each time is based on.
- **The edges of the map.** Places that acted on the Great Kings belong on the map even at its edge, or a power loses part of who it was:
  - **Dilmun and the Gulf.** Dilmun (Bahrain) was Babylonia's in this period, under a Kassite governor, so it starts as Babylonia's land, with a Gulf sea zone from Ur that Elam's coast also touches. It gives Babylonia its sea and its route towards Magan's copper; trade (decided 21 October 2026) gives that route its full meaning ("Economy and resources" under Land, people and economy).
  - **The Kaska lands.** North of Hattusa lived the Kaska, raiders without a king who burned Hattusa itself in the generation before 1346. They had no king but did have chiefs and elders, with whom Hittite kings swore treaties group by group, so they start, like Lukka and the Sutean steppe, under one leader of their own, a chief who rules as any city-state's ruler does and speaks for himself (decided 27 October 2026), and are Hatti's standing threat from the north ("People of the land", "Bands are a character's soldiers"). One leader simplifies them, as a later chief, Pihhuniya, made himself one under Mursili II: he "ruled in the manner of a king", though rule by one man was not the Kaska custom.
  - **The Sutean steppe.** The nomads of the Syrian steppe raided travellers and served as hired fighters. The desert routes from the middle Euphrates cross their land, which starts as desert under one leader of its own, a chief who rules as any city-state's ruler does, its men raiding caravans and hiring out to the vassals, as Biryawaza of Damascus offered Pharaoh "my Habiru and my Suteans" (EA 195; decided 27 October 2026).
  - **Libya and the Shasu.** Two more edge lands under chiefs, as the Kaska, Lukka and the Suteans are (decided 29 October 2026, build order item 11f): Libya west of the Delta, the Tjehenu and Tjemehu, herders and raiders who already appear in the reliefs of Egypt's 18th Dynasty, their great invasions a century and more away; and the Shasu, the herders of the Negev and Edom south-east of Canaan, named in Amenhotep III's lists. Each starts under one leader of its own, with no walls and no market, its men raiding the roads past it and hiring out, Libya on the Delta's western edge and the Shasu on the roads from Egypt to Canaan and to the copper of the Arabah. In the game they bear the period's names ("Places by their own names"): the land of the Tjehenu, and the Shasu of Seir, whose range runs from Seir west into the desert later called the Negev (build order item 17+).
  - **Off the map, as the far ends of routes:** Magan, Punt and Elam's eastern lands beyond Susa; with the economy, Magan and the eastern road are edge markets, and Punt only a door ("What each edge trades").
  - **The western edge:** Ahhiyawa and Millawanda (Miletus) mattered more in the following century; they stay off the map, and with the economy Ahhiyawa is the western edge market, "Keftiu and Ahhiyawa" ("Edge markets"; "The Aegean's far shore" under Ideas).
- **Roads are paid for by those who build them.** A road (build order item 15) is built by the gold and labour put into it. When neighbours build one together, the split is agreed on a sealed tablet and, like every term, is only words. Who owns it is set by "A road belongs to the land it crosses", so building through another's land is an investment he can take, which is why it needs passage rights (item 9) and trust.

Places and dates here are from memory where no source is linked; the builder checks them against the sources and records any doubt.
